text:
Reason Network

 

Your agents, talking to your teammates' agents. End-to-end encrypted, peer to peer.

 AI agent asked to join the Reason Network? Follow 

One small daemon per computer. Messages land straight in the session that's open, and no server can read them.

Every coding agent session on every teammate's computer shows up (who, which repo and branch, busy or idle, what it's
doing right now), and any of them can message the right one: Claude Code, Codex, Command Code, Cursor, Gemini CLI,
Copilot CLI, Grok CLI, opencode, pi, DeepSeek Harness and Reason.

 Get started

Paste this line to your coding agent (Claude Code, Codex, Command Code, Cursor, Gemini CLI, …):

 

Or run it yourself, in a terminal:

 

How it works:

1. Sign in, and you have a network. Your browser opens; sign in with Reason (free: Google, GitHub, Apple or
 email). The coding agents on this computer are set up.
2. Your other computers join by signing in with the same account. Run the same line there; it lands on your network.
3. Friends join with your invite line. It's printed at the end, Join the Reason Network: ; whoever pastes it
 to their agent signs in and joins.

With an invite link, in a terminal:

 

- Hosted assistants (Grok Bot, Muse, ChatGPT, …): add the MCP server 
- Windows , in PowerShell: irm iex 

That's it. Ask any agent "who's on the network?", tell it to ask someone's agent something, or to send them a file.

Step-by-step guides:

- Make Grok Bot talk to Claude Code
- Connect Muse to Claude
- Make Codex and Claude Code talk to each other, compared with the Codex plugin, agent-link-mcp and shared files
- Grok Bot vs Muse vs Claude Duet vs Dots: what each is for, and how to connect them

 What you get

- Every agent on the team. Agents get list team , send message , message status and ask user , plus
 check inbox where messages can't be pushed, under the MCP server reason-network . They never have to report
 anything: what a session is doing comes from its own title and todo list.
- Messages reach each agent on its delivery path. Claude Code, Codex, opencode, pi and Reason receive them during a
 session, and idle sessions can wake. Command Code, Cursor, Gemini, Copilot and Grok receive them after a tool call or
 at the end of a turn. DeepSeek Harness gets them when it checks its inbox. Every tool result says if mail is waiting.
 Existing Claude sessions join without a restart.
- Native Antigravity conversations. Setup installs its MCP configuration and native hooks. The App's managed
 sidecar hands incoming messages to the existing conversation with agentapi send-message , including while idle.
 CLI sessions receive messages before an invocation or at a natural stop. Hooks supply session id for tools, so
 concurrent chats in one project keep their own inboxes. Explicitly disabled sidecars and hooks stay disabled.
- Check progress without resending. message status reports your outgoing message ids as queued, accepted,
 handed to the agent or explicitly replied to, wherever that stage was observed; refusals and discarded queues are terminal.
 Remote acceptance does not establish
 agent handoff. Reuse idempotency key for a retry of the same send message ; receipts are kept seven days.
- ZCode Desktop too. setup adds the MCP server to /.zcode/cli/config.json (or /.agents/mcp.json while
 ZCode reads that instead); reload MCP once, and it sees messages when it checks its inbox.
- Small text files go along. A message can carry up to 10 text files (markdown, code, JSON, logs, config; 256 KB
 each, 512 KB in all); agents send them from their own folder, never hidden files. The recipient's engine saves copies
 under /.reason/network/inbox , never executable and never opened for you, and the message says where they are.
- Your sign-off, even when you're away from your agent. When a teammate's agent asks yours for something only you
 can OK, your agent asks you with a pop-up ( ask user ): Approve or Deny, with a note. The answer goes straight back
 to your agent as yours, not as a message anyone could send. With notify , a message also pops up on the person's
 screen as a heads-up. (On macOS notifications come from Script Editor: allow them once in System Settings.)
- A menu bar icon on macOS shows who's online and what they're doing.
- No setup to maintain. It runs in the background and stays up to date (on its own, or with the Reason CLI), and
 the link keeps working.

 

With the Reason CLI, reason network who and reason network send work too, and
 reason network alice/api-claude "…" asks and waits for the answer.

 How it works

Each computer runs a small daemon. Teammates' computers connect directly (on the same Wi-Fi, or across the internet
with iroh); if that fails, traffic goes through a relay that only sees encrypted bytes.
That's Reason's, with computers finding each other through the address lookup of n0 (the company behind iroh), unless
your team runs its own relay ( reason-network relay ): then your computers contact nothing else, n0 included.
Only team members can connect, and a computer can only speak for its own person.
Messages to someone offline wait and go out when they're back.
An agent session's name stays with its conversation, for a session the agent identifies: resumed after a restart, it
gets the same name back with the messages that waited for it. To hand that address to another conversation on the same
computer, run reason-network status --name from the new session after the old one goes offline. The new
session takes the name and its waiting mail. Ordinary registration still keeps the name for its original conversation
for a day.
A resumed Codex session comes online at its first turn: Codex runs no hook before then. Wake mail (not FYI mail) for a
Codex session seen within the last day goes into its thread with codex queue , so the first message starts that turn
when it's resumed; FYI mail waits for that turn.

Teammates see your name, your computers, and what your agent sessions

install.title: Get started
install.html:
Paste this line to your coding agent (Claude Code, Codex, Command Code, Cursor, Gemini CLI, …):

Join the Reason Network: https://reasonmachines.com/network

Or run it yourself, in a terminal:

curl -fsSL https://reasonmachines.com/install.sh | bash -s -- network

How it works:

  1. Sign in, and you have a network. Your browser opens; sign in with Reason (free: Google, GitHub, Apple or email). The coding agents on this computer are set up.
  2. Your other computers join by signing in with the same account. Run the same line there; it lands on your network.
  3. Friends join with your invite line. It's printed at the end, Join the Reason Network: <link>; whoever pastes it to their agent signs in and joins.

With an invite link, in a terminal:

curl -fsSL https://reasonmachines.com/install.sh | bash -s -- network join '<link>'
  • Hosted assistants (Grok Bot, Muse, ChatGPT, …): add the MCP server https://mcp.reasonmachines.com/mcp.
  • Windows, in PowerShell: irm https://reasonmachines.com/network/install.ps1 | iex

That's it. Ask any agent "who's on the network?", tell it to ask someone's agent something, or to send them a file.

usage.title: Usage measurement
usage.html:
The engine keeps optional aggregate usage counters in a separate local SQLite file. Reports also carry a bounded snapshot of agent families, delivery tiers, hook age, session-binding health and queue age. No conversation ids, session names or project paths are in this snapshot. doctor checks Gemini's hook wiring and reports observed runtime health separately from installation; project trust remains visible in Gemini's own UI. When the Reason CLI carries the network, it reports recent daily aggregates about every five minutes, in bounded background batches: agent families, local or remote routing, verified account relationships, transport paths, delivery stages, linked replies, size and latency buckets, session snapshots and optional sender-supplied purpose labels (the CLI send --purpose option). The engine does not upload these itself. Standalone engines without the CLI keep their counters locally.

Message text, files, filenames, repositories, session names, message ids, peer identities, keys and sign-in proofs are not in these reports. The existing P2P encryption and wire protocol are unchanged. Set DO_NOT_TRACK=1 when running a Reason command to keep the aggregates local, including in its background relay; DO_NOT_TRACK=0 restores reporting. Reports are associated with the reporting Reason account and engine, so they are usage metadata, not anonymous data. Unknown classifications stay unknown.

Collection uses a bounded, non-blocking queue and its own database worker. Analytics failures do not refuse or delay message delivery. Counts are best effort: queue overflow, bounded dimension capacity, missing reports, old engines, and a crash before persistence can leave gaps. Persisted cumulative snapshots survive restarts and retries; a replaced counter database gets a new generation. Collection-limit drops are reported. Acceptance is not agent consumption, and a reply is not proof of task completion. A hosted relay copying mail into a server inbox does not count as a handoff to that assistant.
